title: Week 07 - Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis
text:
This week we move beyond single-variable summaries into bivariate (two variables) and multivariate (three or more variables) analysis. Understanding relationships between variables is the foundation of data-driven insight and predictive modeling.
By the end of this week you should be able to:

Compute and interpret correlation coefficients
Visualize relationships between two continuous variables
Analyze relationships involving categorical variables
Build and interpret a correlation matrix
Visualize three or more variables simultaneously

2. Continuous vs. Continuous

2.1 Scatter Plot
The scatter plot is the most direct way to visualize a relationship between two numeric variables.

data(mpg)

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "tomato") +
  labs(
    title = "Engine Displacement vs Highway MPG",
    x = "Engine Displacement (L)",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











2.2 Pearson Correlation
The Pearson correlation coefficient (r) measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship. It ranges from −1 to +1:

r = 1: perfect positive linear relationship
r = 0: no linear relationship
r = −1: perfect negative linear relationship


cor_val <- cor(mpg$displ, mpg$hwy)
cat("Pearson r:", round(cor_val, 3), "\n")

Pearson r: -0.766 



# Correlation test with p-value
cor.test(mpg$displ, mpg$hwy)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  mpg$displ and mpg$hwy
t = -18.151, df = 232, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.8142727 -0.7072539
sample estimates:
     cor 
-0.76602 



Interpretation: A negative correlation confirms that larger engines tend to have worse fuel efficiency. A p-value below 0.05 indicates this relationship is statistically significant.


Caution: Correlation measures linear association only. Always pair it with a scatter plot — two variables can have a strong non-linear relationship but a near-zero Pearson r.

3. Continuous vs. Categorical

3.1 Grouped Boxplot

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = reorder(class, hwy, median), y = hwy, fill = class)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Highway MPG by Vehicle Class",
    x = "Class",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










3.2 Grouped Density Plot

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy, fill = drv)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Highway MPG Distribution by Drive Type",
    x = "Highway MPG",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Drive Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










3.3 Violin Plot
A violin plot combines a boxplot with a density estimate to show the full distribution shape.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, y = hwy, fill = drv)) +
  geom_violin(trim = FALSE, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white", show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Highway MPG by Drive Type (Violin + Boxplot)",
    x = "Drive Type",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

6. Multivariate Visualization

6.1 Encoding a Third Variable with Color or Size

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class, size = cyl)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Displacement vs MPG (Color = Class, Size = Cylinders)",
    x = "Displacement (L)",
    y = "Highway MPG",
    color = "Class",
    size = "Cylinders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










6.2 Faceted Scatter Plots
Facets allow you to visualize a relationship across subgroups.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Displacement vs MPG by Drive Type, Faceted by Year",
    x = "Displacement (L)",
    y = "Highway MPG",
    color = "Drive Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











6.3 Scatterplot Matrix with GGally
A scatterplot matrix shows all pairwise relationships at once — great for an initial multivariate overview.

  select(displ, cyl, cty, hwy, class) %>%
  ggpairs(
    aes(color = class, alpha = 0.5),
    upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", size = 3)),
    lower = list(continuous = wrap("points", alpha = 0.3))
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot Matrix of Key MPG Variables")

title: Week 07 - Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis
text:
Key Takeaways

Always visualize relationships before computing statistics.
Pearson r only captures linear relationships — check with a scatter plot.
Boxplots and violin plots are powerful for comparing a numeric variable across groups.
Use proportional bar charts (position = "fill") when comparing categorical distributions of unequal group sizes.
Correlation matrices and scatterplot matrices (ggpairs) are efficient for exploring many variables at once.
Facets are your best tool for adding a third variable to a bivariate plot without cluttering it.

title: Week 05 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
1. Recap: What is EDA?
Exploratory Data Analysis is the process of using statistical and visual tools to understand the structure of your data before modeling. It helps you:

Detect errors or anomalies
Understand variable distributions
Discover relationships between variables
Formulate hypotheses

title: Week 05 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
2. Describing Distributions
A distribution describes how values of a variable are spread. Key characteristics:

Shape: symmetric, left-skewed, right-skewed, bimodal
Center: mean, median
Spread: standard deviation, IQR, range
Outliers: unusual observations far from the bulk of the data

title: Week 05 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
3. Visualizing Distributions

3.1 Histogram
A histogram groups continuous values into bins and shows their frequency.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Highway MPG",
    x = "Highway Miles Per Gallon",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








What to look for:

Is the distribution symmetric or skewed?
Are there multiple peaks (bimodal)?
Are there gaps or extreme values?



3.2 Density Plot
A density plot is a smoothed version of the histogram, useful for comparing groups.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Density of Highway MPG",
    x = "Highway MPG",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










3.3 Boxplot
Boxplots show the five-number summary: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum — and flag potential outliers.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy, fill = class)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Highway MPG by Vehicle Class",
    x = "Class",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

title: Week 05 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
4. Outlier Detection
Outliers can be legitimate extreme values or data entry errors. A common rule is the IQR method:

Lower fence: Q1 − 1.5 × IQR
Upper fence: Q3 + 1.5 × IQR


Q1 <- quantile(mpg$hwy, 0.25)
Q3 <- quantile(mpg$hwy, 0.75)
IQR_val <- Q3 - Q1

lower <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR_val
upper <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR_val

outliers <- mpg %>% filter(hwy < lower | hwy > upper)
cat("Number of outliers:", nrow(outliers), "\n")

title: Week 05 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
5. Data Transformation
When data is strongly skewed, transformations can help normalize it for analysis and modeling.

5.1 Log Transformation

# Simulate right-skewed data
set.seed(42)
skewed_data <- tibble(x = exp(rnorm(500, mean = 3, sd = 1)))

# Original vs log-transformed
p1 <- ggplot(skewed_data, aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "salmon", color = "white", bins = 30) +
  labs(title = "Original (Right-Skewed)", x = "x") +
  theme_minimal()

p2 <- ggplot(skewed_data, aes(x = log(x))) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "white", bins = 30) +
  labs(title = "Log-Transformed", x = "log(x)") +
  theme_minimal()

library(patchwork)
p1 + p2

Key Takeaways

Always visualize distributions before computing statistics.
The mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is more robust.
Use boxplots to compare groups and spot outliers simultaneously.
Log transformation is effective for right-skewed data.
Grouped summaries reveal patterns that overall summaries hide.

  mutate(dose = factor(dose))

Dose represents treatment levels rather than a continuous variable, so it should be a factor for proper grouping.

title: Lab 2 - Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Recode supplement labels

tg_clean <- tg_clean %>%
  mutate(supp = recode(supp, "OJ" = "Orange Juice", "VC" = "Ascorbic Acid"))

Full labels make plots easier to read without needing to look up abbreviations.

title: Lab 2 - Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Create derived variable

title: Lab 2 - Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Tooth Length Distribution

  geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = "#3498DB", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(tg_clean$len), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Tooth Length", x = "Tooth Length", y = "Count")








The distribution is approximately symmetric. The mean and median are close, with a considerable spread suggesting treatment effects explain much of the variation.

text:
Supplement Frequency

ggplot(tg_clean, aes(x = supp, fill = supp)) +
  geom_bar(width = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Orange Juice" = "#F39C12", "Ascorbic Acid" = "#2980B9")) +
  labs(title = "Supplement Type Distribution", x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Lab 2 - Exploratory Data Analysis

Each dose level has 20 observations — a balanced design.

title: Lab 2 - Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Dose vs Tooth Length
I expected higher doses to produce longer teeth since vitamin C supports tissue growth.

ggplot(tg_clean, aes(x = dose, y = len, fill = dose)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1ABC9C", "#3498DB", "#9B59B6")) +
  labs(title = "Tooth Length by Dose", x = "Dose (mg)", y = "Tooth Length") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Tooth length clearly increases with dosage, confirming the expectation. The relationship is monotonic and strong.

title: Lab 2 - Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Supplement vs Tooth Length
I expected Orange Juice to be slightly more effective than Ascorbic Acid.

ggplot(tg_clean, aes(x = supp, y = len, fill = supp)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Orange Juice" = "#F39C12", "Ascorbic Acid" = "#2980B9")) +
  labs(title = "Tooth Length by Supplement", x = NULL, y = "Tooth Length") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Orange Juice shows a moderately higher median, but the distributions overlap. The effect is weaker than the dose effect.

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
EDA Mindset
Is iterative, investigative and visual.
Expect: -Go back and forth between steps -Revise assumptions -Discover data issues late in the process -Ask better questions as you learn more

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Understanding the context
Before touching the data understand: -Where did the data come from -Why was it collected - Who or what does each row represent? -What decisions will this data support?
Key questions -Is this observational or experimental data? -Are there known biases? -Is time involved -Are there units, definitions, or domain rules?
Poor context understanding leads to correct analysis of the wrong problem.

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Data Validation (Trust but verify)
Validation answers one core question:
Is this data structurally and logically valid?
This step focuses on correctness, not insight.

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Structural Validation
-Do all columns exist? -Are data types correct -Are there unexpected nulls? -Are identifieres unique when they should be?

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Logical Validation
-Are values within expected ranges? -Do dates make sense chronologically? -Do relationships between variables violate domain rules?
RED FLAGS:
Negative ages Future timestamps Duplicate IDs Impossible combination of values

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Data Cleaning(Fixing What’s Broken)
Cleaning addresses errors, inconsistencies, and noise.
Typical tasks:
-Handling missing values -Fixing inconsistent labels or categories -Correcting obvious data entry errors -Removing or flagging duplicates
Important principle:
Cleaning should be conservative and documented.
Avoid “fixing” data unless:
-You know the cause -The correction is defensible -you preserve original values when possible

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Data Massaging (Making Data Usable)
Massaging prepares data for analysis and exploration, not modeling.
This step is about shape and representation.
Common activities:
-Renaming variables for clarity -Creating derived variables -Converting units or scales -Reshaping data (wide - Long) -Standardizing formats (dates, categories, text)
Key idea: Clean data can still be unusable massaging makes it analysis-ready.

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
section: Univariate Exploration (One Variable at a Time)
text:
Univariate Exploration (One Variable at a Time)
Now you start learning what the data looks like.
For each variable, ask:
-What values occur? -What is typical? -What is extreme? -What is missing?
Conceptually
Numeric variables distribution, spread, skewness
Categorical variables frequency, dominance, rarity
This step builds baseline intuition.

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Bivariate Exploration (Relationships)
Next, explore how variables relate to each other.
Ask questions like:
-Does one variable change with another? -Are there strong associations? -Are relationships linear, nonlinear, or absent?
Focus on:
Direction Strength Consistency Exceptions
Many insights live in relationships, not individual variables.

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Multivariate Exploration (Context Matters)
Multivariate analysis looks at relationships conditiones on other variables.
This helps answer:
Does this relationship hold across groups? Is this pattern driven by a subset? Are there interaction effects?
This step often reveals:
Hidden structure Cofounding Variables Simpson’s paradox-type effects

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Outliers and Anomalies (Signal or Noise?)
Outliers are not automatically bad.
Ask: Are they errors? Are they rare but valid cases? Do they represent a different process?
Important distinction: Outlier extreme but valid Anomaly inconsistent with data-generating process
Never remove outliers without understanding them.

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Assumptions checking
Before modeling, EDA helps you check:
Distributional assumptions Independence Stationarity (for time-based data) Linearity or monotonicity
This step informs:
Feature engineering Model Choice Transformation needs

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
EDA is Iterative
EDA does not end cleanly.
You will:
Discover issues late Revisit Cleaning Create new variables mid-analysis change direction based on findings
This is normal and expected.

title: Week 04 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Key Takeaways
EDA is about understanding, not proving
Most errors are found before modeling

By the end of this week you should be able to:

title: Week 06 - ggplot
text:
This week we take a deep dive into ggplot2, R’s most powerful and flexible visualization library. ggplot2 is built on the Grammar of Graphics, a principled framework for building plots layer by layer.
By the end of this week you should be able to:

Understand the grammar of graphics and the ggplot() structure
Map variables to aesthetics (color, size, shape, etc.)
Use a variety of geom_* functions
Customize themes, labels, scales, and facets
Combine multiple plots

title: Week 06 - ggplot
text:
1. The Grammar of Graphics
Every ggplot2 plot is built from the same components:







Component
Description




Data
The dataset being visualized


Aesthetics (aes)
Mappings from variables to visual properties


Geoms
The geometric objects drawn (points, bars, lines)


Stats
Statistical transformations (counts, smoothing)


Scales
Controls over axes, colors, sizes


Facets
Splitting the plot into subplots


Theme
Non-data visual elements (fonts, background)



The basic syntax is always:
ggplot(data = <DATA>, aes(<MAPPINGS>)) +
  geom_<TYPE>(<OPTIONS>)

title: Week 06 - ggplot
text:
3. Core Geoms

3.1 Scatter Plot — geom_point()
Used to visualize the relationship between two continuous variables.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Engine Displacement vs Highway MPG",
    x = "Engine Displacement (L)",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










3.2 Adding Color by Group

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Engine Displacement vs Highway MPG by Class",
    x = "Engine Displacement (L)",
    y = "Highway MPG",
    color = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










3.3 Line Plot — geom_line()
Useful for time series or ordered data.

# Average MPG by year and drive type
mpg %>%
  group_by(year, drv) %>%
  summarise(mean_hwy = mean(hwy), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_hwy, color = drv, group = drv)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Highway MPG Over Time by Drive Type",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Highway MPG",
    color = "Drive Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










3.4 Bar Chart — geom_bar() and geom_col()
geom_bar() counts observations. geom_col() uses a pre-computed value.

# Count of cars by class
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = fct_infreq(class), fill = class)) +
  geom_bar(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Vehicles by Class",
    x = "Vehicle Class",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









# Pre-computed averages with geom_col
mpg %>%
  group_by(class) %>%
  summarise(mean_hwy = mean(hwy)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(class, mean_hwy), y = mean_hwy, fill = class)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Average Highway MPG by Class", x = "Class", y = "Mean MPG") +
  theme_minimal()










3.5 Histogram — geom_histogram()

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Highway MPG Distribution", x = "Highway MPG", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()










3.6 Boxplot — geom_boxplot()

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, y = hwy, fill = drv)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Highway MPG by Drive Type", x = "Drive Type", y = "Highway MPG") +
  theme_minimal()










3.7 Smooth Line — geom_smooth()
Adds a regression line or LOESS smoother.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "gray50") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "tomato", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Engine Displacement vs Highway MPG (with Linear Fit)",
    x = "Displacement (L)",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Week 06 - ggplot
text:
4. Aesthetics in Depth
Aesthetics can be mapped (tied to a variable) or set (fixed for all observations).

# Mapped: color varies by class
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point()







# Set: all points are red
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(color = "red")








Common aesthetics: color, fill, size, shape, alpha, linetype.

title: Week 06 - ggplot
text:
5. Scales
Scales control how aesthetic mappings look.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 7, by = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Custom Color Scale and Axis Breaks") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Week 06 - ggplot
text:
6. Facets
Facets split a plot into subplots based on one or two variables.

# facet_wrap: one variable
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ class, ncol = 3) +
  labs(title = "Displacement vs MPG Faceted by Class") +
  theme_minimal()









# facet_grid: two variables
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(drv ~ cyl) +
  labs(title = "Faceted by Drive Type (rows) and Cylinders (cols)") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Week 06 - ggplot
text:
7. Themes and Labels

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy, fill = class)) +
  geom_violin(show.legend = FALSE, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white", show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Highway MPG Distribution by Vehicle Class",
    subtitle = "Violin plot with embedded boxplot",
    caption  = "Source: ggplot2::mpg dataset",
    x = "Vehicle Class",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray40"),
    axis.text.x   = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )








Built-in themes: theme_minimal(), theme_classic(), theme_bw(), theme_light(), theme_dark().

title: Week 06 - ggplot
text:
8. Combining Plots with patchwork

library(patchwork)

p1 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", bins = 20) +
  labs(title = "Histogram") + theme_minimal()

p2 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "salmon") +
  labs(title = "Boxplot") + theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

p1 + p2

title: Week 06 - ggplot
text:
Key Takeaways

ggplot2 builds plots in layers using the Grammar of Graphics.
Always start with ggplot(data, aes(...)) then add geoms.
Aesthetic mappings link variables to visual properties; setting fixes them.
Use facet_wrap() or facet_grid() to create small multiples.
theme_*() functions quickly change the overall look of a plot.
patchwork makes combining multiple plots easy.
